clue.text: Killer spared the rod, initially, by one who may use it

indicators.note: initially asks for the opening letter of each of the three words spared, the and rod

parts.note: an angler is a fisherman, who uses a rod

explanation.surface: A murderer who was never caned as a child turns the tables on whoever wields the cane.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes the first letters of 'spared the rod', giving STR; 'it' then points back to the rod, here a fishing rod.
explanation.definitionFit: A strangler is a murderer who kills by throttling, so the word names one kind of killer.

clue.text: Housemaster's thrown in lake by former headmaster

indicators.note: something thrown into a lake ends up inside it, so these letters go inside the lake word

parts.note: a tarn is a small mountain lake
split as house's abbreviation HO plus master's, MA'S (Master of Arts), with the apostrophe ignored
former means old, as in an old flame

explanation.surface: A housemaster gets dumped in the lake by a retired headmaster, a school prank in reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housemaster's' must be split: HO for house and MA'S for master's (MA, Master of Arts). Thomas Arnold was the celebrated headmaster of Rugby School, 1828-41.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Arnold was the reforming head of Rugby School, the most famous Victorian school head.

clue.text: Protected like centrally curled-up creature raptor mauled badly

indicators.note: badly signals that the letters of raptor mauled are set out in a disordered way

explanation.surface: A small creature curled up tight is savaged by a bird of prey.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'centrally curled-up creature' is the puzzle's hidden picture: an ARMADILLO curled round the centre of the grid, through 17a, 18d, 21a and 17d. An armadillo is protected by bony plates.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a hard plated shell, like an armadillo or a tank, is to be shielded by plating.

clue.text: Comedian and broadcaster finally recalling game ref nearly abandoned at Forest

indicators.note: abandoned suggests something done wildly and without restraint, so these letters are scrambled
nearly means the word ref loses its final letter
finally asks for the closing letter of the word recalling

parts.note: Arden is the Forest of Arden, the setting of As You Like It

explanation.surface: A broadcaster remembers a match at Nottingham Forest that the referee called off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forest' looks like Nottingham Forest, the football club; it is ARDEN. 'abandoned' scrambles GAME RE (ref without its last letter) into GRAEME.
explanation.definitionFit: Graeme Garden is a British comic writer and performer, one of The Goodies and a regular on radio panel shows.

clue.text: Shed in emergency room after chucking model girl?

indicators.note: in says the shed word, once cut down, goes inside the hospital letters

parts.note: ER is the abbreviation for a hospital emergency room

indicators.note: after chucking means the model letter is thrown away from the shed word

parts.note: a lean-to is a shed built against a wall
T is a model, as in the Ford Model T

explanation.surface: Someone sheds tears in casualty after dumping a fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' reads as a verb but is a noun, a garden building; 'after chucking' drops the model, and 'in' sets what is left inside the hospital letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eleanor is a woman's first name, so it is an example of a girl; the question mark flags the definition by example.

clue.text: New hospital's no parking — I put in a complaint

indicators.note: put in says the single letter goes inside the rearranged letters
new signals that the letters are made into a fresh arrangement
no means the parking letter is removed from the word

parts.note: read as the plural hospitals, keeping the final S
P is the abbreviation for parking, as on road signs

explanation.surface: Someone files a grievance that the new hospital has no car park.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges HOSITALS (hospitals with P removed by 'no') and 'put in' places I inside the result.
explanation.definitionFit: Halitosis, bad breath, is a medical complaint in the sense of a minor ailment.

clue.text: King taking princess up to club's playing fields …

parts.note: GR stands for Georgius Rex, King George

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the princess letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: Di is Princess Diana, a crossword staple
read as clubs; irons are golf clubs

explanation.surface: A king takes a princess along to the club's sports grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns DI into ID in this down light. The ellipsis leads into 8 down, which continues the royal story.
explanation.definitionFit: A gridiron is an American football field, so gridirons are playing fields for that sport.

clue.text: … with his princes following him as descendants

indicators.note: following says the later letters come after the king's letters

parts.note: him refers back to the king in 7 down, GR
and means with, as in bread and butter
a king's princes are his sons

explanation.surface: The king's sons trail after him as his heirs.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 7 down: 'him' is that clue's King, and 'following' puts the rest after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Grandsons are a person's children's sons, so they are descendants two generations down.

clue.text: Queen wearing sari — rather improper in an African meeting place

indicators.note: wearing means the queen letters are wrapped inside the garment letters
improper suggests the letters are not in their proper order

explanation.surface: A queen in a sari strikes an unseemly note at a gathering in Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'improper' scrambles the garment and 'rather' into TAHRIRSARE, and 'wearing' wraps that round the queen. Tahrir Square in Cairo was the focus of Egypt's 2011 protests.
explanation.definitionFit: Tahrir Square in Cairo is the plaza where Egyptians gathered in the 2011 uprising.

clue.text: Those sharing a place with poor Thomas More after Henry deserted him

indicators.note: poor suggests the letters are in a sorry state, so they are rearranged
deserted says the king's letter leaves the name

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for henry, the unit of inductance

explanation.surface: Poor Sir Thomas More was abandoned by Henry VIII and shut away in the Tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deserted' drops H from THOMAS MORE, leaving TOMASMORE, which 'poor' rearranges. Henry here is the unit symbol H, though the surface reads as Henry VIII.
explanation.definitionFit: Roommates are people living in the same room or flat, so they share a place.

clue.text: What may be revealed in full-frontal entertainment?

definitions.text: What may be revealed in full-frontal entertainment?

parts.words: What may be revealed in full-frontal entertainment?
parts.note: the surface hints at a nude show, but the letters of fronTAL ENTertainment literally conceal a word for a gift or knack

explanation.surface: A nude stage show may expose more than gifts for performing.
explanation.walkthrough: The word TALENT sits concealed in 'fronTAL ENTertainment', so the clue describes its own wordplay: a talent that is hidden. A rude show may also reveal a performer's unsuspected gifts.
explanation.definitionFit: A gift nobody knew someone had is a concealed ability, here literally tucked inside two clue words.

clue.text: Housework by wife primarily, we hear, following holiday to China?

indicators.note: following says the later letters come after the holiday letters

parts.note: vac is short for vacation, a holiday

indicators.note: we hear says the letter's spoken name is written out instead
primarily asks for the first letter of the word wife

parts.note: Ming is the Chinese dynasty famous for porcelain, which is also called china

explanation.surface: Doing the chores, mostly the wife's job, after a trip to China.
explanation.walkthrough: 'primarily' takes W from wife, and 'we hear' writes it as said: double U, UU. 'China' is MING, the dynasty and its porcelain.
explanation.definitionFit: Vacuuming, cleaning floors with a vacuum cleaner, is a typical household chore.

clue.text: Is Dr Cameron right getting upset with man on his hobby horse?

indicators.note: getting upset suggests the letters are knocked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: Dr Cameron, the senior doctor of the old TV drama Dr Finlay's Casebook, gets upset at a man obsessed with his pet subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'man on his hobby horse' reads as a bore with a fixation, but morris dancers really do perform with hobby horses. Morris dancing is an English folk dance.
explanation.definitionFit: Some English folk dancers perform with a hobby horse, a figure of a horse worn by a dancer.

clue.text: Wee girl almost collapsed due to endless weariness

indicators.note: almost means the girl word loses its final letter

parts.note: lassie is a Scottish word for a girl, wee being Scots for small

indicators.note: collapsed suggests the letters fall into a heap and are rearranged
endless means the word to loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A little girl has fainted from never-ending exhaustion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims LASSIE to LASSI; 'endless' cuts to down to T and 'collapsed' turns DUE T into TUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lassitude is a state of physical or mental tiredness, a synonym for weariness.

clue.text: Take axe to country area with low-level growth

parts.note: to scrub a plan is to cancel it, to take an axe to it
land means a country, as in a foreign land

explanation.surface: Clearing a stretch of countryside of its shrubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take axe to' suggests chopping trees; here it means cancel, SCRUB.
explanation.definitionFit: Scrubland is ground covered with stunted bushes and low shrubs rather than trees.

clue.text: Headless cat appearing in phrase about body parts

indicators.note: appearing in says the cat letters show up inside the other letters
about here means astir or around, so the letters are moved about
headless means the cat word loses its first letter

parts.note: a lynx is a wild cat

explanation.surface: A beheaded cat turns up in a turn of phrase about anatomy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' scrambles the phrase into PHARES, a sense some solvers dispute; 'Headless' beheads the cat and 'appearing in' slips it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The pharynx is the throat cavity behind the mouth, an anatomical part; this is its plural.

clue.text: Area right in front of male member

indicators.note: in front of says the first letters come before the male letter

explanation.surface: A spot just ahead of a man's private parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' tempts a rude reading, which is the joke; it is a limb.
explanation.definitionFit: An arm is a limb, and member is an old word for a limb of the body.

clue.text: The whole boring item's broadcast

indicators.note: broadcast means the word is spoken out, so it is the sound that counts

parts.note: an awl is a pointed tool for boring holes

explanation.surface: Everything about this dull object gets aired.
explanation.walkthrough: 'boring' looks like dull; it means making holes, as an awl does.
explanation.definitionFit: All means everything, the entire amount, so it stands for the whole.

clue.text: Nuts from 1,012 years ago

parts.note: the puzzle appeared in 2012, and 1,012 years earlier was the year 1000 AD
M is the Roman numeral for 1000 and AD marks a year of the Christian era

explanation.surface: Lunacy dating back a millennium.
explanation.walkthrough: The puzzle was published in 2012, so 1,012 years earlier is AD 1000, written M AD.
explanation.definitionFit: Nuts is slang for crazy, so it means mad.

clue.text: Nearly everybody's calm drinking hot drink

indicators.note: nearly means the word for everybody loses its last letter

parts.note: all means everybody; the possessive adds no letter

indicators.note: drinking means the calm word takes the hot letter inside it

parts.note: cool means calm, as in keep your cool
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: Almost everyone stays cool while sipping something hot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' trims the everybody word; 'drinking' has calm swallow hot, making COHOL. 'hot drink' looks like the definition, but only 'drink' is.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcohol is a general name for intoxicating liquor, so it is drink in that sense.

clue.text: Gin drunk in water somewhere in France

indicators.note: in says the rearranged letters go inside the river name

parts.note: the Avon is a river, a stretch of water

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters are reeling and rearranged

explanation.surface: Gin mixed with water, somewhere on the continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gin drunk in water' suggests a mixer; 'water' is the English river, and 'drunk' scrambles the gin into IGN, which 'in' puts inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Avignon is a city in Provence in southern France, famous for its papal palace.

clue.text: Top drug, one essential after heart transplant

indicators.note: a heart transplant swaps the middle of the word, so its central letter is replaced

parts.note: LSD is the hallucinogenic drug
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A prime drug, essential for recovery after heart surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'after heart transplant' replaces the middle letter of LSD, S, with I for one.
explanation.definitionFit: A lid is the top or cover of a container.

clue.text: Wrongly has one confused on last of the three R's

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: confused means the letters are mixed up
last of asks for the final letter of the word the

parts.note: three letter Rs written out

explanation.surface: A muddled pupil wrongly applies the last of the three Rs: reading, writing and arithmetic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges the pool into NERROR. The three R's are reading, writing and arithmetic, the old basics of schooling.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in error is doing it by mistake, so the phrase means wrongly.

clue.text: See 9
See 4
See 3
See 2
Late riser hit the shops?

indicators.note: hit suggests the letters are struck and knocked about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone who gets up late heads off to go shopping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hit the shops' reads as a phrase meaning go shopping; 'hit' is the anagram signal and 'the shops?' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Retailers are businesses that sell goods to the public, so collectively they are the shops.

clue.text: See 11
Learning from publication about sport

indicators.note: about means the publication word goes around the sport letters

parts.note: an edition is a published version of a book or paper
RU is rugby union, the sport

explanation.surface: Picking up knowledge from a magazine about a sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link and 'about' wraps the publication round the sport; 'sport' is the usual crossword shorthand for rugby union.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudition is deep scholarship gained by study, a synonym for learning.

clue.text: See 13
Relatives' piano died? That's awfully sad

definitions.note: the plural possessive reads as plain plural relatives

parts.note: a grand is a grand piano
D is the abbreviation for died, as in family trees

indicators.note: awfully suggests the letters are badly placed and so rearranged

explanation.surface: The family piano has died, which is terribly sad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'awfully' rearranges the sad into DAS. 'Relatives'' looks like a possessive owning the piano, but is just the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Granddads are grandfathers, the older members of a family, so they are relatives.
